messages.author: 11167693f0a5e891
messages.subject: workaround for cut() function?
parts:
Hi all,
I am new to Stan, trying to convert a model from OpenBugs to Stan.
In the model I have experimental error that I want to include in the estimate, but without the "true" measurement to be estimated/optimized
(see The Bugs Book section 9.4 p202).

So in BUGS this is:

  for (i in 1:N){
    x.observed[i] ~ dnorm(x.estimate[i], tau.x[i])
    x.cut[i] <- cut(x.estimate[i])

    y.hat[i] <- a + b * x.cut[i]
    y[i] ~ dnorm(y.hat[i], tau.y)
  }


Since there is not cut() function in stan I am wondering how to to this.

Would substracting from lp__ have the same effect as the cut() function in BUGS in this case?

  for (i in 1:N){
    x_observed[i] ~ normal(x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);
    lp__ -= normal_log(x_observed[i], x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);

    y_hat[i] <- a + b * x_estimate[i]
    y[i] ~ normal( y_hat[i], sigma_y)
   }

Is this the "correct" way of doing this?

   Many Thanks,
       Stephan

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] workaround for cut() function?
parts:
Not having the BUGS book to hand, could you provide
a bit more of the model and indicate what's data and
what's a parameter and what the log probability function
works out to?

If you can write the log probability function down, you
can code it in Stan. I'm not sure all the uses of cut
in BUGS correspond to a well-formed model.

In your subtraction example, everything gets cut out
and it's like

Stan lets you do something like cut for predictive inference
in the generated quantities block, but there's no way to feed
this back into sampling for other parameters. That is, you
need to cut from some parameters all the way down the directed
model to the leaves.

Your suggestion:

> x_observed[i] ~ normal(x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);
> lp__ -= normal_log(x_observed[i], x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);
>

won't work because that's just an inefficient way of writing
a no-op. That is, the model will have the same probability function
with both of these lines removed.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] workaround for cut() function?
parts:
On Saturday, May 11, 2013 4:22:29 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
I think cut() is bad news.  Martyn Plummer and I have had some discussions about it.

The cut function seems dubious to me too, but if you wanted to do something like that in Stan, I think you can just do

lp__ <- lp__ - whatever;

where whatever is the sum of the log-likelihood contributions that you don't want to influence the posterior.

Ben

messages.author: 11167693f0a5e891
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] workaround for cut() function?
parts:
Here is the complete model for the example:

#-------
data{
   int<lower=0> N; # number of data points
   real x_observed[N]; # experimentally observed x
   real sigma_x[N]; # experimental error for observed x
   real y[N];
}
parameters{
   real a;
   real b;
   real sigma_y[N];
   real y_hat[N];
   real x_estimate[N]; # random variable incorporating the
                       # experimental uncertainty into the model
               # this could also be just a temporary variable
}
  
model{

for (i in 1:N){
    x_observed[i] ~ normal(x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);
    lp__ -= normal_log(x_observed[i], x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);

    y_hat[i] <- a + b * x_estimate[i]
    y[i] ~ normal( y_hat[i], sigma_y)
   }
}

#--------

The experimental error x_sigma for x_observed varies a lot between data points. The idea is to use x_estimate as a random variable to sample from the distribution of x_observed during the simulation, which should be reflected in the confidence intervals for parameters a and b.
I do not want to get the x_estimate that gives me the best fit to y, I am interested how the confidence intervals for a and b change as I run multiple experiments, each experiment giving me a different set of x_observed (but there is only one set of y measurements).
The idea is to run multiple simulations with the same y but different sets of x_observable, and see which one has the tightest confidence intervals for a and b.
You mentioned that what I am doing is an inefficient way of doing a no-op, which is kinda the idea (I think), as long as x_estimate[i] is varying according to the experimental uncertainty for data point x_observed[i].

Maybe there is a better way of doing this, I am coming over from the BUGS way of doing this and trying to figure out how to do this in Stan. Any suggestions and critique are welcome.

  Many Thanks,
       S.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] workaround for cut() function?
parts:
On 5/11/13 4:45 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Saturday, May 11, 2013 4:22:29 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>
> I think cut() is bad news. Martyn Plummer and I have had some discussions about it.
>
>
> The cut function seems dubious to me too, but if you wanted to do something like that in Stan, I think you can just do
>
> |
> lp__ <- lp__ - whatever;
> |
>
> where whatever is the sum of the log-likelihood contributions that you don't want to influence the posterior.

In general you can indeed create the log probability
function however you want, including by substracting terms out.

Just be careful that if you write something like the original
poster suggested,
x_observed[i] ~ normal(x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);

lp__ <- lp__ - normal_log(x_observed[i], x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);

it's equivalent to just removing both statements, because they
exactly cancel each other out. That's because the first statement
is just shorthand for

lp__ <- lp__ + normal_log(x_observed[i], x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);

so after executing both, lp__ is back to where it started.
All the derivatives will get evaluated and will just cancel
out, too. All of this only up to arithmetic precision, of course.

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] workaround for cut() function?
parts:
Hi.  The reason why I (and others) perceive "cut" as bad news is because when you do "cut," you are no longer doing Bayesian inference.  To put it another way, if it's really true that you don't want inference going from A to B, I don't think you want it going from B to A either.  Joint distributions go both ways.
A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] workaround for cut() function?
parts:
On 5/11/13 4:56 PM, sreiling wrote:
> Here is the complete model for the example:

I meant the BUGS model with the cut!

I literally meant it behaves as a no-op.
The model

> model{
> for (i in 1:N){
> x_observed[i] ~ normal(x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);
> lp__ -= normal_log(x_observed[i], x_estimate[i], sigma_x[i]);
>
> y_hat[i] <- a + b * x_estimate[i]
> y[i] ~ normal( y_hat[i], sigma_y)
> }
> }
is equivalent to the model that removes the first two statements:

> model{
> for (i in 1:N){

> y_hat[i] <- a + b * x_estimate[i]
> y[i] ~ normal( y_hat[i], sigma_y)
> }
> }

You do need semicolons in Stan, though, so the above won't actually compile.
You don't need to declare intermediate variables like y_hat unless you
want to see them. Instead, you can rewrite the above model as just this:

model {
y ~ normal(a + b * x_estimate, sigma_y);
}

It will be more efficient.

> The experimental error x_sigma for x_observed varies a lot between data points. The idea is to use x_estimate as a
> random variable to sample from the distribution of x_observed during the simulation, which should be reflected in the
> confidence intervals for parameters a and b.
> I do not want to get the x_estimate that gives me the best fit to y, I am interested how the confidence intervals for a
> and b change as I run multiple experiments, each experiment giving me a different set of x_observed (but there is only
> one set of y measurements).
> The idea is to run multiple simulations with the same y but different sets of x_observable, and see which one has the
> tightest confidence intervals for a and b.
> You mentioned that what I am doing is an inefficient way of doing a no-op, which is kinda the idea (I think), as long as
> x_estimate[i] is varying according to the experimental uncertainty for data point x_observed[i].

I'm not familiar with this approach to modeling measurement error.
I did read the linked slides and they match your description, so I
think I see what's going on.

> Maybe there is a better way of doing this, I am coming over from the BUGS way of doing this and trying to figure out how
> to do this in Stan. Any suggestions and critique are welcome.

As Andrew pointed out in another reply, if you have a joint probability,
information flows both ways just through the laws of conditional
probabilities. All a Stan model does is specify a
joint probability p(y,theta|x) over data y, parameters theta, and covariates
(also data) x. We then sample from p(theta|y,x). If you can formulate the model
as a proper joint probability density, then it can probably be coded in Stan.
If not, then it definitely won't be codeable in Stan.

The only thing like the BUGS cut operator that Stan supports is
in predictive inference. You can fit the model as you usually would,
then define predicted quantities in the generated quantities block that
can depend on the values of parameters. This information does not flow
back into the model in a semi-supervised way. There's an example in
the manual for HMMs where this makes a difference.

- Bob
